speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the matter, and will give my hon. friend the information at a later date.

The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
Public Works-Chargeable to income-Harbours and Rivers-Prince Edward Island, $39,700.
Will the minister tell us what amount was spent upon these services last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Kootenay, Minister of Public Works) :

speechtext: Was there any expenditure last year from the vote for "Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $14,000"?	.
Yes, the sum of $3,742.20 was expended.

How was the $14,000 made up, may I ask? Was it put in because that amount was in the estimates

Supply-Public Works
last year, or does it consist of items that have been submitted by various officers of the department?
It is a general contingency vote carried from year to year and is used during the year for repairs that become necessary from time to time. We really cannot tell in advance what these repairs may be.

The point that was drawn to my attention was this. While the amount of $14,000 is put in for Prince Edward Island that sum is very seldom, if ever, spent. Last year the total expenditure was only some $3,000 odd. It has been intimated to me that the other items cover very well, very liberally, all the expenditure that is likely, or is possible, in Prince Edward Island under this vote for the next twelve months. Someone, I understand, has gone over the requirements of the Island with a good deal of care, and has put in a separate item for each possible work that may be necessary during the next twelve months. Therefore, I am told, the item of $14,000 will not be required-it never, or seldom, is required and the committee could save that money by striking the item out of the estimates this year.

The item of $14,000 is for contingencies that may occur. It is true that last year the expenditure was only $3,742, but I do not think the present item should be disturbed; it is apparently the amount the staff think should be carried for a contingency of that kind.

But this amount of $14,000 is not recommended by any engineer of the department, or anyone who has examined the situation; I understand it is just put in as a sort of " cover all " charge; you may need it and you may not. My information is that some officer of the department has gone very thoroughly over the harbours and rivers of Prince Edward Island; that he has set out in detail what is required; and that he has been very generous in his estimate and has covered all the requirements in the various items totalling the sum of $39,700. Now the $14,000 is seldom, if ever, spent. In this case it is not likely to be spent at all: I would suggest to the minister under these circumstances it would have a better appearance if he agreed to the item of $14,000 coming off; or that $10,000 of the amount come off, leaving $4,000 for little incidentals that might possibly crop up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a similar provision, I think, in the case of most of the other provinces. It is really an emer-gehcy item; it is not a thing that can be specified at the beginning of the year. And even if the money was not spent last year, circumstances might make it very desirable that it should be disbursed this year.

I understand the probable necessities of the other maritime provinces are much greater than those of the province of Prince Edward Island; in the case of New Brunswick there is a contingency vote of $40,000. I understand that quite often it is necessary to spend a good portion of the vote for a province, to repair damages caused by storms. But I am told that the officer who made up the estimate went over all these works and that he has taken possibilities as well as probabilities into his consideration. Now the expenditure under this item is about $2,000 to $4,000 annually. My point is that it is hardly worth while voting the $14,000 when there is no likelihood of spending the money. Something might, arise eventually demanding an expenditure, -'something did occur last year because $3,000 was spent. Under the circumstances I think it would be very reasonable to put in a sum of $4,000 for contingencies, and reduce the vote by $10,000.

It is quite evident from the remarks of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that he is not very well acquainted with maritime province conditions; he comes from a part of the country where the conditions would not enable him to have very much, knowledge in regard to matters of this kind. Owing to the fact that the province in question is an island it contains quite a number of harbours, and in those harbours are important public works. No man can foretell when a storm may come up and inflict very great damage on a number of these works. Therefore a prudent government, one having the interest of the country at heart, will most naturally and necessarily have an amount of this kind to provide for such contingencies. The necessity for the expenditure may not arise for years; but at any time storms may occur resulting in very great damage, and it would be very vital to have that damage repaired with the utmost promptitude. Really it is true economy to have the money available for that purpose; therefore this item has
Supply-Public Works

appeared in the estimates for many years. It is not a new vote, and if the money is not wanted it will not be expended, and no harm will be done. I think that if my hon. friend understood the conditions as they actually exist in Prince Edward Island, he would not object to this vote.

The storm which my
hon. friend fears might happen and do considerable damage, might occur anywhere; but we could always make provision for cases of that kind. Suppose you had an earthquake, or a heavy storm, and damage to the amount of $50,000 or $100,000 was done; that could immediately be taken care of.
In what way?

By Governor General's warrant. It has been done in the past, time and again. This system of warrants is designed to take care of unforeseen sudden expenditure, and there is no object in continuing the vote of $14,000. The minister might just as well put it in at $100,000 or $150,000. Experience has shown that $2,000 or $3,000 is necessary. Granting that you may be called upon to make a heavy unforeseen expenditure when the House is not in session, it is always open to the minister to go to the Governor General and get a warrant, and come down at the next session of parliament, as has been done time and again, and ask for the money.

I do not think there should be any misunderstanding regarding this vote. It is in the usual form and was carried last year and the year previous. It is a vote for contingencies which may arise, which cannot toe foretold. A similar vote was passed the other day in regard to the province of Nova Scotia, $60,000 for contingencies. In regard to this particular vote, I am told that $2,200 has already been required as expenditures which should be made under that vote this year. Beyond that, we have no knowledge as to what will be required. It is a usual vote, not only in this department but almost in every department, for unforeseen expenditures.

I do not know whether the principle is a good or a bad one. I find the estimates show contingent votes for harbours and rivers, which run into a very large sum of money. For Nova Scotia we voted $60,000 for contingencies, not knowing how the money is going to be spent. For Prince Edward Island we are asked to vote $14,000; New Brunswick, $40,000; Quebec, $75,000; Ontario, $65,000; Manitoba, $15,000; Saskatchewan and Alberta, $20,000 between them; and British Columbia, $95,000-all these votes for contingencies. That is a very substantial amount of money, and there are no particulars given-none can be given, the circumstances have not arisen for the expenditure of even a fraction of it. Why can we not remove this large amount of money from the estimates, and, if money is necessary during the twelvemonth, get it as we did in other cases, by Governor General's warrant?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not unfortunate that when my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) was in a (better position to influence this item, he did not apply these principles? He has selected a regrettable moment to do it. He should have done it when he had the power.
I do not know that it is regrettable. I bring it up at the present time, and if I did not notice it or my attention was not called to it last year, it has certainly been called to it this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Evidently.

Not by a man far from Nova Scotia, but by a gentleman from Nova Scotia, who pointed out the item. If the principle is wrong it is a good time

to correct it; if it is right, let us confirm it.

friend's informant?

The fact that I did not
cal! attention to it last year, or the year before, is no reason for saying, if it is wrong, that we should not put it right now. South Wellington apparently has a stricken conscience and I challenge him to name a man from Nova Scoitia of outstanding ability-

Or in any other province-who objects to any item in the Public Works' estimates which have been presented to this parliament. Harbours and rivers-New Brunswick, $66,700.
I see an item here "Portage river-repairs to breakwater $1,200". In what county is Portage river?
In Kent county.

I understand there are
two Portage rivers in adjacent parishes. Perhaps they are in adjacent counties. I would like to know the parish. I have had an inquiry about it.

Parish of Carleton, Kent
County.

I have not the
parish. Portage river is a small stream
entering the Northumberland straits about five miles from Point Sapin and six miles north of Kouchibouguac, population 150.

Has any policy been arrived at with respect to the question of provincial wharves on tidal waters in New Brunswick? If I understand the matter aright, the scheme adopted by my hon. friend's friends of the provincial government of New Brunswick is to unload upon the Dominion treasury the maintenance and upkeep of all the public wharves that have been built in that province since the beginning of time, and thus relieve themselves of a burden which they voluntarily took upon themselves in days gone by. If the minister will question the officials of his department, he will find that a very prodigal policy has been pursued in the past by both governments with respect to building public wharves in New Brunswick in tidal waters, which wharves, for the most part, have been built purely for political purposes. This was especially true on the river St. John during the regime of the Laurier government down to 1911 when a former member of this House represented that constituency as a supporter of that government. If you will travel up and down the river St. John in the counties of Queen's and Sunbury, you will find two or three wharves in the same locality, one built by the Dominion, one by the province and another by one or the other as a high water wharf or a low water wharf, as the case may be. At the present time, all are in a state of disrepair, and the provincial government have refused to carry out the policy which was instituted twenty-five or thirty years ago with respect to building these wharves, and to keep their wharves in repair. Similarly, during the war, owing to the exigencies of the finances of the country, the Dominion authorities allowed many of their wharves to fall into disrepair-one could very well understand that. But lately, an effort has been made on the part of the provincial authorities by the Foster government to unload on the Dominion all the upkeep and maintenance of these provincial wharves in tidal waters. Just the other day, Hon. Mr. Foster was a visitor to Ottawa. I do not know that his visit to the capital synchronized with the vacancy which has recently occurred in the Senate or not, but he paid a visit to Ottawa, and on his return to New Brunswick he announced that the Dominion authorities had agreed to take over from the province all the provincial wharves in tidal waters. I should like to have from the minister a
Supply-Public Works

statement as to what policy has been decided upon in that regard. I would point out to him also the duplication of services by the two governments in the past, and, having regard to that, would ask what is proposed to be done in the future. While I am on my feet I should like to point out to the minister that, in this appropriation of $66,700, there is not one dollar for the repair of a single Dominion wharf in the water of the St. John river or its tributaries, although many important wharves are to be found in that locality.
Will the hon. member kindly state how many Dominion wharves are on that river?

If I had time, I could recall them; but at the very least, there must be a dozen. In my constituency of Sunbury, there is one at Oromocto, one at Mangerville, one at Burton and one at Sheffield, a very important wharf.

Is there on the St.
John river one wharf owned by the Dominion government?
Yes.
There is not one. I was eight years in charge of the wharves there, and there is none.

I will not take any back seat to the hon. gentleman. I have already pointed out four in the county of Sunbury, and if I had time to think of them, I could point out half a dozen more. There is a public wharf at Gagetown, a very important point on the river St. John, where during the season of navigation, a very large quantity of produce and lumber is shipped each year. That is a Dominion wharf. I know that because I was instrumental in having some minor repairs done to that wharf last year by the Dominion authorities.
In these estimates there is not a dollar for a single wharf on the St. John river, although there are at least a dozen in that locality. There is not a single dollar for a wharf in the bay of Fundy waters, except at three points in the county of Charlotte. The entire vote is being appropriated for the north shore counties, and that is not a fair distribution. With respect to the appropriation of $40,000 generally for harbours and rivers in New Brunswick, I do not object to the principle of that blanket appropriation, except to make this observation-that, in times gone by, a very much larger appropriation was [Mr. Hanson.J
inserted in the estimates, and it was used as occasion required, not altogether on business principles. I do not, however, object to the amount of $40,000 in the estimate this year, if the minister will say that attention will be given to those Dominion wharves where, I know, attention is required.
Does my hon. friend object to wharves in tidal waters of New Brunswick being taken over by the Dominion government the same as has been done in the case of wharves in other provinces?

If that is a general
policy that has been adopted by this Government-

My hon. friend misunderstands me. The wharves in the other provinces have not been taken over by this Government; they have been maintained by the Dominion government for many years, and the province of New Brunswick is the only province in the whole Dominion that has been compelled to keep up wharves in tidal waters. Does my hon. friend object to the province of New Brunswick being treated in the same manner as the other provinces?

I do not understand
that to be the case. If my hon. friend will, on his authority as a minister of the Crown, state that that is the case, then I would submit that New Brunswick should be placed in no different position from that of any other province. But if that be not the case, I will object to hon. gentlemen opposite loading on to the Dominion the burden which the province of New Brunswick voluntarily assumed, and which it should keep up because it voluntarily assumed the burden.

Representations have been made during the last two or three years to the Dominion government by the provincial government of New Brunswick, asking that this government take over and control the wharf service in New Brunswick. Heretofore there has been a dual service, which apparently came into vogue many years ago. The matter was under consideration by the late government and, I believe, it had reached a certain stage where an order would probably have been presented with that idea in view. The policy was not adopted; but for the information of the committee, I may say that recently I have had representations from the government

Supply-Public Works
of New Biunswick following up the representations which they made in 1919 and 1920; the matter is receiving consideration, but the final decision has not been reached.

How much of last
year's estimate of $118,000 was spent, and how much of last year's estimate of $40,000 was spent?
Of the $40,000, $11,600 odd was spent.

Plow much was spent
of the total?
Amount spent,
Who is the engineer in charge of the Public Works Department in New Brunswick?
Mr. Stead.
Has the agency at Chatham been closed?
Yes.
And the whole coast line, including the river St. John, is now under his jurisdiction?
Yes.

I do not see anything in the estimates this year for any construction on the island of Grand Manan. This is_ the largest island in the bay of Fundy, with the largest population, and there are works there that undoubtedly require attention.

I understand
that there was no report from the engineer, when the estimates were prepared, as to the necessity for any construction there.
What are the instructions given to the engineer? Does he voluntarily make a report, or is he requested to go over the situation?
He voluntarily reports from time to time upon the requirements of his district.
There is a vote of $1,500 for Leonardville and $1,700 for Welchpool, both for "repairs to wharf." Are these wharves in Charlotte county?
They are both in Charlotte county.

Have any representations been made to the department, on behalf of the people of Grand Manan and the neighbouring islands, urging the necessity for the construction of breakwaters in all or any of these islands?
I shall be glad to look into the question and give my hon. friend the information. I have not the facts at the moment.

I should be very much surprised to learn that no representations of this kind have been made to the department, for I believe that it was generally understood, prior to the last election, that in the event of the present administration being returned to power construction would be proceeded with at once on breakwaters at some or all of these islands.
The promise was made.

Well, at any rate, the
people generally understood that. Now, the people have carried out their part of the' programme, and it rests with the Government to fulfil any promises that may have been made on their behalf. These islands form a part of the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and they are isolated from the mainland. The island of Campobello and Deer island are situated five miles from the nearest point on the mainland out in Passamaquoddy bay and the island of Grand Manan is twenty miles away from the mainland out in Atlantic ocean. The people of these islands depend entirely on fishing for a living. Any hon. member who knows anything at all about this industry is aware of the hardships and the disadvantages generally which those who are engaged in it have to endure. The village of Castalia, on the island of Grand Manan, was at one time a prosperous fishing community, but owing to the disadvantages under which the people laboured the young men went over to the United States where they could engage in their occupation under more favourable conditions. The heavy seas and storms from the Atlantic, beating upon the island, have destroyed the waterfront. The people, in the event of a storm, have to moor their boats two miles from home, and this entails a serious hardship upon them. Nature has provided a splendid foundation for a breakwater and all that is required is for the Government to carry it to completion. The people believe that the young men will come back if they are given an opportunity to engage in the industry under proper conditions. The breakwater could

Supply-Public Works

be completed at little expense and it would carry out any promises that may have been made to the people. At Woodwards Cove some years ago the government undertook the construction of a breakwater and completed one section, and the people are desirous of having the work carried to completion. On Deer island, at the cove above Wilson's Beach, which is the central part of the island, the fishermen work under more favourable circumstances. They do not require a great breakwater, as they have a magnificent cove in which to moor their boats. But the fishermen to-day have to carry their fish along the beach to the houses, the water being too shallow for them to moor their boats near shore. They are anxious to have the department of Public Works do at least a week's dredging so that they may have ample mooring accommodation. The work would cost comparatively little and would meet the requirements of those who engage in fishing in that part of the country. The upper portion of Deer island, as far back as the oldest inhabitants can recollect, has never received its due share of public works. The people desire to have a wharf or a breakwater there. Either would be satisfactory to them, and it is imperative that the construction be begun at as early a date as possible in order to enable the fishermen to carry on their industry. Only a small amount would be necessary to provide permanent facilities, and the people have been wanting the work done for a considerable time now. I see that for Nova Scotia the estimates provide $182,680 while for New Brunswick the amount is only $66,700, just about one-third. Surely the Government can afford to implement the promise they made the people in that portion of Charlotte county. I should be gratified if the minister would give me definite assurance that these new public works, which would not cost a great deal and which are absolutely necessary if these people are to carry on their business, will be provided.
I would call the attention of the minister and of the committee to the character of the campaign carried on by the Liberal candidate in Charlotte county, New Brunswick, during the last election.
Carried.

The item is not carried. As hon. gentlemen are aware who know the geography of that locality, a very large
portion of the population of the county depends on the fishing industry for a livelihood. I am intimately acquainted with the place, as it happens to be my native county, and I have lived there a good many years. During the last general election, Mr. W. F. Todd, the defeated Liberal candidate in Charlotte county, carried on a campaign throughout the island parishes, and promised a wharf or breakwater at practically every fishing hamlet in the county.
Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hanson) make any promises of a similar kind in his county?
No, I did not make any.
What about the Transcontinental railway? The hon. member for York-Sunbury wanted the divisional point which is in my town transferred to his own town, and he campaigned for that change.

I would point out to the minister and the House that what I have referred to was a straight bid for votes on a bribery principle. We have heard of such cases in days gone by in connection with our election campaigns. I would point out further that no attempt whatever has been made to implement what the Liberal candidate so lavishly promised on that occasion. Some of those promises, I haVe no doubt, were made in good faith; others undoubtedly were made with the intent and purpose of influencing the electors. That practice has a degenerating influence on our public life, and-[DOT]
Oh, oh.

Some of my hon. friends opposite laugh, I suppose because it has been such a common practice by them in the past, especially in New Brunswick. I would point out to the minister that some of these promises were made by Mr. W. F. Todd, the Liberal candidate in my constituency, and have not been fulfilled, I think the minister would be doing a duty to the people down there if he would endeavour to have those promises redeemed.
Were the wharves and breakwaters which my hon. friend says were promised, necessary to the county of Charlotte, which he speaks of as being his native county?

Some few were; most of them were not.

Supply-Public Works

Unfortunately Mr. Todd is not here to defend himself against this very serious charge. But my hon. friend was not content with making this charge against Mr. Todd alone; he says that all the members of this House from the province of New Brunswick took the same course during their respective campaigns.
I did not say that. I said that that course had been pursued in the past by hon. gentlemen from New Brunswick.
Members of this House at present?
No.

While making allowance for the fact that my hon. friend is a young member of this House, yet I feel it is neither fair nor courageous on his part- and I think the House will agree with me- to make these charges against his opponents without bringing evidence to substantiate them. My friend Mr. Todd was a member of this House for many years, and several hon. members will recall the splendid reputation which he enjoyed. Before my hon. friend charges his opponents with making, during the course of his campaign, promises verging on bribery, he should at least have the courtesy and courage to bring some evidence before this committee upon which he bases his charges. On the contrary he has not offered the slightest evidence in support of what he alleges.

Mr. Chairman, I have great pleasure in bringing to your notice a specific instance. Just previous to the general election Mr. Todd arrived at Grand Manan, accompanied by a number of henchmen, including Mr. B. M. Hill, chief engineer of highways for New BrunsWifek. They not only told the people of Grand Manan that they would build them a motor speedway, but Mr. Hill, I am informed, actually went around among the electors-and, be it known, Mr. Hill was defeated in the provincial arena-and engaged men to work upon that road, ostensibly to make a survey, but practically to go to work on the road. That was all very well until election day; we have never heard about the matter since.

My hon. friend, just as I expected, has shifted his ground entirely. He transfers his charge from Mr. Todd to Mr. Hill, the superintendent of local highways in New Brunswick. My hon. friend knows, as does everyone else in New Bruns-

wick, that Mr. Hill is an employee of the local government there. No doubt he went down to the county of Charlotte for the same purpose that he has visited all the other counties in the province, to build highways; and he has helped to build many magnificent highways in New Brunswick. But the building of provincial highways has nothing whatever to do with the construction of breakwaters and wharves in the county of Charlotte.
The money out of which Mr. Hill proposed to build the highways was to come from the federal grant, which certainly has a very important hearing on Dominion politics.
That is all expended by the local government under the superintendence of Mr. Hill.

Mr. HAN.SON: The Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) challenged me to give a list of the places where those supporting him had made definite promises to carry out public works in the county of Charlotte prior to the last election. I have in my hand a list of those places.
I did not say anything about those who were supporting me.

I will let you have a list anyway. The first place as to which Mr. Todd, and those supporting him, made such a promise, and the most important public work to which he had relation, was the completion of the 'breakwater at Castalia, Parish of Grand Manan. Mr. Todd was there and personally looked over the ground and told the people he would have the breakwater carried to completion. The second place was at Welshpool-
Did my hon. friend say Castalia?

Yes Castalia, Parish of Grand Manan. At Welshpool Mr. Todd personally promised that dredging would be done forthwith. The third place where a promise of a public work was made, was at the upper end of Deer island, near Lord's cove Where he personally-
Has my hon. friend any objection to the members in this part of the Chamber hearing his statement? We cannot hear him at all in this quarter.

I shall be delighted to oblige my hon. friend. As I say the third promise related to a wharf or breakwater at the upper end of Deer island, just beyond Lord's cove. Mr. Todd promised a wharf or a breakwater; I am not sure that he did not promise them both. The fourth place was at Seeley basin, in the parish of Pennfield, where a wharf site was actually located before the 6th December. I dare say, if I had the time, I could give my hon. friend a dozen other places.
Is my hon. friend speaking from hearsay, or was he present and heard the statements referred to?
The hon. member knows I was not there.
My hon. friend is repeating what somebody told him.
I am speaking from information which I know to be correct.
I would like the hon. gentleman to give a little further information.
I do not know, Sir, that you have any right to cross-examine me.

I am not cross-examining my hon. friend. Apparently he is a hostile witness and a cross-examination of that type of witness is sometimes dangerous. However, I would like my hon. friend to be kind enough-he having volunteered very valuable information to the committee in regard to the attitude of Mr. Todd during the last election campaign regarding the construction of wharves and breakwaters or both, in his county-to state whether the public works suggested by Mr. Todd as being desirable are necessary for the inhabitants of the particular localities mentioned.

They are not in the estimates and therefore in the opinion of the Government they cannot be necessary. If my hon. friend wants an answer I would refer him to the officers of the Public Works Department who are the technical advisers of the Government. It is not my duty, it is not even my privilege, to advise my hon. friend.

My hon. friend apparently misunderstood my question.

Supply-Public Works
I do not think so.

My hon. friend is a native of Charlotte county and he has a very close acquaintance with its requirements, as well as with the requirements of the county of York which he represents. I would like, therefore, if he would be good enough to tell the committee whether, in his opinion, the construction of the public works in question is necessary for the benefit of the inhabitants of the respective localities referred to? If he says it is, I am sure the Minister of Public Works will give the matter his very careful consideration?
I will put this proposition to the minister: If I answer his question will he undertake to carry out the recommendation that I make? Then I will answer his question.

I am very deeply interested in the information my hon. friend has given to the committee. It is the first I have heard with respect to these localities requiring accommodation of the kind referred to. I would be very glad indeed if my hon. friend would inform us whether these works are absolutely necessary. If they are, I will be very glad, seeing that I represent the province of New Brunswick, to give the matter my very best consideration, and see if something can be done to meet the requirements in question.

As the representative of the county of Charlotte I will answer the question and say that, I think these works are absolutely necessary. They should be built in the interest of the people of the county, and any promises that were made at the last election should be carried out. If Mr. Todd made the promises referred to I think he was perfectly right in doing so; the works are really needed by the people, the fishermen and others, who carry on their occupations in those localities. I will back the minister up if he will undertake these works and carry them to completion. However, as no amounts have been provided in the estimates I can see no chance of this being done.
There is the sum of $40,000 in the estimates.
That will not go far towards building a breakwater in Castalia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am a little interested whenever I hear of any one breaking a contract and not keeping faith. Now if
anybody, either Liberal or Conservative, promised to build wharves or piers, or anything of the kind, as a means of getting votes, that is wrong, that is bribery-call it what you like-and therefore I cannot excuse it. But I am going to ask my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) as to the nature of these promises. Did I understand correctly, that Mr. Todd promised that these things would be done if Mr. Grimmer was elected?

The questibn of the hon.
minister answers itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does not allege that any such promise was made; therefore there was no breach of contract.

I call attention again to the very large item of $40,000 in these estimates. The total estimate is $66,000. There is an amount of $40,000 unspecified. I do not think it is good business to put such a large amount for unspecified work in the estimates. I noted what the minister had to say in regard to a similar item for Prince Edward Island. I wish to point out that the total estimates in respect to Prince Edward Island were $40,000 and the unspecified amount was $14,000. In the other case, the total amount was $66,000 and unspecified $40,000, a disproportionate amount.

I do not want to delay the estimate, but following up what the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has stated, I think the minister should consider the objection. See the opportunity it gives the minister, if the vote goes through as it stands. Last year $11,000 was spent and $29,000 not spent. If similar conditions exist this year the minister will have under that general vote $29,000. For his own protection he should change this systeim. Every government heeler in New Brunswick will 'be after him to spend this money. At least, I venture the opinion that some will be after him. They will be chasing the minister, and all sorts of reports will come to him that $2,000 should be spent here, $3,000 another place, and $5,000 another place. Parliament has nothing to say in regard to the expenditure, we are leaving it in the hands of the minister to say when and where he will spend the money. He will undoubtedly he importuned and for his own protection it would be far better if the amount were reduced. There is no emergency that cannot be taken care of by Governor General's warrant, and the minister should welcome my
Supply-Public Works

suggestion. I know that this system has obtained in 'the past, why not correct it for the future? I ask the minister if he will not announce a reduction Of $10,000 in the total vote of $66,000. We have an item, "Contingencies, improvements and repairs generally, $40,000." We are asked to give the money without knowing whether it is going to be spent, or where. It is an improper principle.

I will cite a few items of expenditure last year under this vote, and my hon. friend will see the fallacy of his argument when he says that a Governor General's warrant be passed on every occasion of this kind. We find that at Chance Harbour $100 was spent; at Cognac, $18; Leonard'ville Wharf, $25.20; Mill Point, $543.77. Many items, large and small, come up for consideration and conditions Occur from time to time where the engineers or the officials are required to report on certain matters and make expenditures. I think the hon. member will see how cumbersome it would be if we had to obtain Governor General's warrants on every occasion of thi's kind. A contingent vote to take care of unforeseen conditions is not unusual in the Public Works Department or in any other department. The vote last year was the same amount as this year; I have not the information as to the preceding year, but I imagine the vote was somewhat similar. The expenditures vary from year to year, as one can well understand, and I see no reason Why the vote should be reduced. It will not be expended if it is not required.
What was the total expenditure in these items last year, and what need is there for having a much larger expenditure this year?

The total expenditure last year was $11,666, out of a vote for contingencies of $40,000. I would not and could not advise the committee that the expenditure would be the same as last year. No one can foretell that. I see no reason to change the vote.

I see the point in what the minister says, that there is a lot of small payments which have to be made, but I think $10,000 or $15,000 would be sufficient for all purposes. I wish to test the matter and take the view of the committee, and for that purpose I am going to move to reduce the item. I do not desire to reduce it in respect of New Brunswick only, and I want to avoid making a motion as
[Mr. Guthrie.!
each item comes up, and my amendment will be simply to take the feeling of the committee upon this question. I move that the item of $40,000 for repairs and improvements generally be reduced to $20,000. That will allow the minister a very substantial amount and a large margin, to carry on incidental repairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment of my hon. friend, I think, shows a failure to appreciate the very spirit and purpose of the resolution. It is an emergency vote for something that cannot be anticipated. The most we can say is that it may not be needed. The past experience has shown that when it was not needed it was not spent, but, surely, it is well to have a margin of safety in that case, and the figures the minister brings down are precisely the same as last year's. I think it would be a mistake to depart from the rule laid down in the past; I do not think the hon. member has shown any good reason for reducing the vote.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) negatived: Yeas 24; Nays 79.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-Quebec, $396,980.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee that this appropriation be taken up in detail item by item?
No.

Surely my hon. friends are not going to ask the committee to pass a batch of details consisting of probably forty different items, without a word from the minister. I am surprised that the minister himself did not offer to give to the committee an explanation of some of these items. How much of the total appropriation of $423,160 of last year was spent? How much of the appropriation of $75,000 of last year for harbours and rivers generally was spent?

The total expenditure from last year's appropriation was $254,557.56. Of the appropriation of $75,000 for harbours and rivers generally last year, the expenditure was $62,881. That in itself shows that these items vary from year to year. In Quebec last year we practically expended the sum set aside for contingencies.

The minister and the Government will note that, out of an appropriation of about $423,000, only

Supply-Public Works
$254,000, or very little over one-half, was spent. The minister is asking this year, on the policy and plea of retrenchment and economy, an increase of about $142,000 over the expenditure of last year. We ought to have an explanation of this very large increase.

I do not think my hon. friend would suggest that the estimates and expenditures made last year should govern and rule the committee this year. The estimates are prepared in the department on the knowledge and advice of the officials of the department. We have not found it necessary to ask for as large a sum as was asked for last year. This year we are asking for $396,980 against $423,100 last year. My hon. friend says that, as the expenditure last year was only $254,000, we should further reduce the amount this year. I do not think he is competent-and I know, as minister, with the time at my disposal, I am not competent-to advise the committee that that should follow. I am taking the advice of the officials of my department, and this would seem to be a reasonable amount for expenditures in the province of Quebec. It is well known to hon. members that, during the war period, undoubtedly, and wisely so, public works were not maintained as they should be in normal times, and the Department of Public Works at this time finds it necessary to make more extensive repairs than probably would have been necessary if the ordinary repairs had been carried on from year to year.

The minister is enunciating a policy of extensive and increased expenditure on public works. He states that during the war there was retrenchment, and that now is the time for expansion. We were led to believe, by the oft-repeated and widely advertised declarations of the Government that this was to be a period of retrenchment.

I think my hon. friend has misunderstood me. I merely stated that, owing to the fact that public works were allowed to fall into disrepair during the war period, it is found necessary now to make larger expenditures on these works in order that we may retain what we have. To do otherwise, would be false economy.

Surely we could run over these items quickly, and the minister could give us a brief explanation of the
reasons for them. The first item, Anse aux Gascons wharf, is a revote of $29,000, only $20,000 of the appropriation of last year of $49,000 having been expended. We should have an explanation of that. And some of the other items are very large.

The $29,000 asked for Anse aux Gascons wharf covers a contract entered into last year. The contract price was $49,000, and the expenditure in 1921-22 was $20,000, so that a revote this year of $29,000 is required to carry out the contract entered into in 192122.

Is the appropriation for repairs and reconstruction of the wharf at Gaspe in the same situation? The appropriation last year was $34,000, and we are asked for a revote of $20,000 this year. Was that under contract?
Yes.
I think there was a contract for the wharf extension and repairs at Grosse Isle quarantine station, but I am not sure. How far has that work been proceeded with?

The vote asked is for repairs to the flooring, replacing of mooring posts in the eastern wharf and extension of eastern wharf. Of the appropriation of $50,000 last year, $15,000 was expended, and the amount lapsed is $9,000. This revote of $26,000 is to complete the work.
Was $15,000 the total expenditure last year on this work?
Yes.
Last year's appropriation was $50,000?
Yes.
Then the total cost of this work when completed is going to be only $41,000 instead of $50,000?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-Ontario, $398,800.

How much was spent
of last year's estimate amounting to $644,700?
Altogether,

What percentage was
spent of the vote of $65,000 for harbours and rivers generally?
Supply-Public Works

The amount
spent was $44,263.

Does the minister intend to put anything in the supplementary estimates for Goderich harbour? He will remember that a deputation waited upon him a few weeks ago. This is the only harbour between Port McNicoll and Sarnia, and last year 22,000,000 bushels of grain passed through it. The harbour should be dredged to enable big boats to turn round. Sometimes vessels have remained in the harbour for as long as ten days getting unloaded.
The representations made by my hon. friend and by the deputation are receiving consideration, but I am not in a position to advise as to what will be put in the estimates.

The question of the Goderich harbour has been before the House many times during the last ten years. The position became rather acute four or five years ago. It was felt that during the war the expenditure would hardly be justified. My recollection is that what is required in Goderich harbour will take a considerable amount of money. I believe that the expenditure is urgently needed. My hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. Black) knows the situation better than I do, but I have heard the matter discussed by various delegations, and I know something about the railroad that runs through the city of Guelph where I live and which is dependent for a large part of its trade on the grain that comes through the Goderich harbour. This harbour, I think, is the only one for large boats on the shores of Lake Huron, from Port McNicoll all the way down. It requires a considerable course of dredging. The chief expenditure is needed for something in the nature of a sea wall to make the harbour safe in stormy weather. At present it is the only port where a ship can put in in stress of weather on the whole of that side of lake Huron, and it is of considerable consequence to mariners in general to have the harbour properly built up and developed, apart altogether from the question of shipping. Goderich is reached now both by the Grand Trunk and by the Canadian Pacific (railways. There are large elevator systems in the locality and a tremendous amount of grain passes through the port. I hope, therefore, that the Government will take the matter up, and when the supplementary estimates come down I shall certainly join with my

hon. friend from South Huron in endeavouring to convince the Government that a substantial expenditure should be made there.

Why do you not make a
motion to that effect?

I see that we are discussing votes for Ontario, and it is rather strange that the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) does not move an amendment to reduce the item for the expenditure of $65,000 on harbours and rivers.
I have explained why.

Since he is appearing before the House as the great economist he might very well do that. He is not only backing up the member for South Huron in urging the necessity for expending this large amount of $398,000 odd in Ontario, but he wants 'the (Government to spend more. . Now, if that vote were asked for New Brunswick or British Columbia, or some other province, my hon. friend would be on his feet immediately, telling the Government that? they were spending too much money. It strikes me that a great deal depends on whose ox is gored, and the hon. member for South Wellington seems to be the most inconsistent gentleman in this House.

It will not take long
to reply to my hon. friend. I am not making any motion in respect of this $65,000 for harbours and rivers generally, in Ontario, for the reason that I have given to the committee. I merely wished to test the opinion of the committee once for all, and apply it to all the items in the estimates. That would save time, and it is final and definite enough for me. I do not object to any expenditure on rivers and harbours in any part of Canada where the expenditure is warranted; I have not once objected to such expenditures in these items. I have however, objected to money being voted for the Government to spend without Parliament knowing how it is to be expended, and that objection was well founded, notwithstanding the vote of the committee.

It is all very well for the hon. member to get up, now that he is in opposition, and be so pious politically:	He
was not quite so pious a few days before the election, however. He got contracts let in the city of Guelph for some $300,000 for militia supplies that were not needed.

For how much?

Supply-Public Works

Nor was he so pious in other things. He should he the last gentleman to rise in hiis place in this House and declare that there should not be one dollar expended without minute details as to how it will be disposed of. The whole trouble with the hon. gentleman is that he is not acquainted with the facts. With regard to the votes in the different provinces for harbours and rivers generally, I do not suppose it would be parliamentary for me to say that my hon. friend's attitude is due to ignorance on his part.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I do say, however, that it is due to lack of knowledge. And that is the whole trouble with him. Now, I know very little about the province of Ontario, but I can conceive the possibility that instead of $65,000 being required for harbours and rivers in that province in the year 1922, the Government may have to spend $150,000. The money, I presume, is voted in order that the public works on the Great Lakes may be repaired when they are destroyed by storms such as we had last night. In the vote for Nova Scotia the committee will see, on page 38 of the Estimates, a sum of $60,000 provided for harbours and rivers generally. Those hon. members who went home late last night and experienced the disagreeable weather we had then, must certainly have realized, if their thoughts were either on the Pacific or on the Atlantic, that some damage was being wrought by the storm on those two great bodies of water. This morning I received telegrams from my own constituency informing me that several public works along the shore were washed away last night; and knowing the nature of those works, I should judge that it would take at least $50,000 to repair them. Of course, the member for South Wellington does not know anything about that; he is a sea lawyer more or less, and he is only arguing this afternoon from hearsay.
The hon. gentleman's remarks are not complimentary to sea lawyers.

Perhaps not, but the hon. member's arguments are advanced only for the sake of opposition to the votes. The minister is quite right in putting these votes in the estimates, because it is impossible for himself or his officials to know just how much Will be required in British
Columbia, Nova Scotia, or any other province. It is good business to have these estimates provided, and it has always been done. The hon. member, I repeat, is objecting only for the sake of opposition and not because he knows what he is talking about.

I do not always agree with my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), but I insist that a larger vote should be placed in the estimates for Goderich harbour than is provided. The Board of Trade at Goderich told me they estimated it would take $400,000 to fix the wharf, but they are only asking this year for about $100,000 to do necessary dredging so that boats can unload as they come in. I have a photograph showing eleven boats laden with grain all waiting to come into the harbour. Some are held back a week at a time.
How much grain was handled at Goderich last year?
Twenty-one million bushels of grain was brought into Goderich harbour last year.

As one of the members from Ontario who supported the amendment to reduce the previous vote, I wish to say to my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) that I did not do so from a spirit of opposition, hut for the reason that the vote last year was only one-third of the amount set apart and to be voted this year. Consequently it seems to me that without some justification for the increased expenditure we ought to cut it down.
Is the hon. member satisfied with my explanation?
With reference to the item for Ontario of $65,000, if it could be shown . it was not needed I would be only too glad to support an amendment to reduce it.
It is impossible to show that it is not needed.

I understand, in respect to the $65,000 item, that last year nearly the whole amount was spent, so perhaps it is reasonable to infer that at least as much will be needed this year. That is the only basis upon which I refrain from objecting to this vote. .

The remarks of the
hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in regard to Goderich harbour, are very well timed, and I thoroughly agree
Supply-Public Works

with his request to the Minister of Public Works to consider the needs of that harbour. Goderich is the one point on lake Huron where the western grain is distributed to the millers of Ontario, and on that account alone deserves the support of this Government. But I would point out to my hon. friend from South Wellington that Goderich is not the natural harbour of refuge for lake Huron. Many old members will recall the awful storm of 1914 when much tonnage and many lives were lost on the Great Lakes. As a result the government of the day started to build a harbour of refuge farther north on the shore of lake Huron, Goderich being a little too far south to supply that needed shelter. Such a harbour of refuge is absolutely necessary for the safety of our mariners, and should be taken into favourable consideration by the minister. The losses on lake Superior and the other Great Lakes recently amply justify the need of more shelter.
I would point out to some members coming from inland ridings that those of us representing ridings with extensive lake frontage realize that these emergency expenditures to which the hon. Minister of Finance referred are at times entirely inadequate. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) referred to harbours destroyed in the recent storm. His remarks apply to lake harbours as well. Wharves that have been allowed to run down during the war years are now in a perilous condition, and in my riding to-day I do not think the wharves can be put in shape for half the emergency vote for the whole province. Therefore I think members from inland ridings should be tolerant of this emergency vote, and also of the vote for Goderich harbour because of the fact, as I have stated, that it is the only grain distributing harbour on the Great Lakes for a large part of Ontario.
I shall be glad to support the minister if he brings forward any vote in his supplementary estimates for a harbour of refuge north of Goderich, because we know that the men on the Great Lakes at the present time have not the protection which they should have against the severe storms which occasionally overwhelm them. If we had another storm similar to that of 1914 there would be again a great loss of life, and this we should prevent if possible by the construction of a harbour of refuge.

I think my hon. friend referred to the fact that 21,000,-

000	bushels of grain comes to Goderich harbour. Is any of that grain unloaded for transportation to other destinations, or is it all distributed to the millers in that section of the province?

As one of those well acquainted with the conditions surrounding Goderich harbour and the adjacent country, I must take exception to the statement of my hon. friend with regard to Goderich harbour as a distributing point. Goderich is the distributing centre for grain for six or seven counties in the western part of Ontario, and I would urge the hon. minister to increase the grant so that these counties may be benefited.

Unfortunately I was called out when the hon. minister stated the total expenditure for last year. I notice the total appropriation for public works charged to income this year is $9,817,319.77; the amount asked last year for this service was $10,871,362.08. Can the minister tell me what the total expenditure was last year in connection with public works charged to income?

My hon. friend is in error. The votes last year for public works totalled $13,188,000, and the amounl expended was $10,283,000.
Mr. BOYS* I thank the hon. minister for the answer, but I do not quite see how I am wrong. I hold in my hand the estimates for 1922, and on page 38 I see the amount to be voted is $10,871,362.08. Of course, I am not including the supplemen-taries. I suppose that accounts for the difference?
Yes.

I would draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a really urgent case which has developed in my riding during the past two weeks, and I am afraid that if something is not done in the way of provision in the Supplementary Estimates the wheels of industry in that part of my constituency will be at least retarded if not entirely tied up.
1	have reference to the harbour at the town of Little Current, on the north channel of Georgian bay. As hon. members no doubt are aware, we have a large coal dock at that point handling from 100,000 to 200,000 tons of coal per annum, coal which is shipped in during the session of navigation and carried northward over the Al-goma Eastern railway to the various industries on that line. Up to two years

Supply-Public Works
ago boats of about 10,000 tons burden could carry the coal to the dock, but owing to the lowering of the water in lake Huron, probably due to the Chicago drainage canal and other causes, the channels of that lake are becoming so low that boats of large draft can no longer go through them. In this connection I should like to read a letter I have received from Mr. G. A. Montgomery, and of which no doubt the minister has a copy in his department:
Dear 'Sir,-The Steamer Collier owned by the Cleveland Cliffs Iron Company. Cleveland. O.. loaded with approximately 5,500 tons of coal for the Spanish River Pulp & Paper Mills, struck while coming to our dock at Little Current on Sunday, April 23rd. The point where the steamer grounded was in mid-channel just off Gibbons Point. Captain Wilson who was in charge of the vessel, claims he was on the ranges when the boat grounded. Steamer was drawing eighteen feet six, but there was only abount eighteen feet two or three inches of water. Damage to the vessel consisted of thirteen frames bent and three plates sprung. This is the seventeenth trip that Capt. Wilson has made to Little Current and he states the Collier was on exactly the same course as followed by him on previous trips. The Coilier is being repaired at Little Current by stopping up the leak with concrete. The Harbour Master at Little Current has been notified of the grounding and I understand he has, in turn, notified the Marine Department.
Following that, I received yesterday and the day before three or four telegrams. Here is one I received from the Soo:
Would appreciate anything you can do in removing danger of navigation at Little Current. Grounding of the steamer Collier already reported to you will have serious effect upon our business. Vessel owners making strenuous objections sending their boats to our dock on account of navigation difficulties that point.
I have also a telegram from the mayor of Little Current, as follows:
On last trip steamer Colilier aground in centre of channel. Bottom badly damaged. Something must be done at once or coal dock wiM have to close to large steamers.
The minister, I think, received a wire yesterday from the owners of the boat at Cleveland, reading as follows:
Cleveland, Ohio, May 16, 1922.
Steamer Collier entering Little Current channel April 23rd struck rock obstruction damaging eleven plates and frames to such extent boat obliged come down light. For drydocking cost of repairs approximately ten thousand dollars. Very necessary obstruction be removed. Considerable pressure is brought upon us from time to time move coal into Little Current as some Canadian owners have refused to carry coal to that place account of constant liability of damage.
A. E. R. Schneider, Cleveland Cliffs Iron Company.
I might say in passing that the Espanola Pulp and Paper Company consumes some
150 tons of coal every twenty-four hours throughout the year. They get all their coal from that dbck, so you can see what this means to them. If something is not done to remove this obstruction, that immense industry and. other industries along the north shore will have to close down. I trust that the minister will have this matter attended to immediately. I might even suggest that the Government dredge, which I believe is now fitting out at Midland, on the Georgian Bay, he taken up to Little Current to do the work, so that these boats can get in. It will be a serious national loss if this work is not done.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-Manitoba, $28,500.

I think this item is very modest in comparison with appropriations that have been made for similar work in some of the other provinces. I think it is entirely inadequate to take care of the situation that has developed in Manitoba. The other day I brought to the attention of the House the fact that the Assiniboine river had overflowed, and that considerable damage had been done. The Prime Minister assured me that this matter was engaging the attention of the Government, that they were endeavouring to find out the actual extent of the damage, and would report later. We really do not know the extent of the damages yet, but the Canadian Pacific Railway has made an estimate, and their figures go to show that from fifteen to twenty thousand acres of arable land have been flooded. We also read in the press that hundreds of men have been engaged night and day trying to stem the waters of the Assiniboine. I believe it is the duty of the Government to compensate these men for the work they have been forced to do, and to reimburse them for any damage they have suffered. I . would suggest that the minister ascertain the extent of the actutal damage as near as he can, and bring in a supplementary estimate to cover it. I might say for the benefit of the House that the overflowing of the Assiniboine river has been a political question in our constituency.
Any promises made?

There have been promises made in the past, and I would suggest to the Government that they do not wait until the eve of an election before compensating these people for the damages they have suffered. The damage has already been done, and now is the time
Supply-Public Works

to take care of it. I was told that last fall engineers had gone over the ground and had made some observations, with what object I do not know; but that is all we have heard about it. I should like to read an extract from a letter signed by " Observer " to the editor of the Daily Graphic, a paper published in Portage la Prairie:
The Assiniboine river is under the Dominion government, not the provincial government. This was duly evidenced during two different elections run by the late government at Ottawa, when they with great earnestness, foresight and sympathy put large gangs of men on the work of building a dyke along the Assiniboine river. The activities, however, appeared to cease on each occasion immediately after the election day was passed.
I have read that just to warn the Government that now is the time to take action, instead of waiting until the eve of an election. I want to plead for the settlers in my constituency, and I hope that the Government will see fit to help them in their extremity.
What was the actual expenditure under this item last year?

For harbours
and rivers generally, $6,341. The total expenditure last year was $27,000.

I am very glad that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has brought up this question of the overflowing of the Assiniboine river, because I had intended to bring it up myself. I am interested in the matter because the Assiniboine river has been overflowing its banks right down through the constituency of Brandon, and has done quite a lot of damage at Virden. The banks have also overflowed at Brandon, and a great deal of inconvenience has been caused, not only to the farmers in the district, but to the people in the city of Brandon itself. I do not know just exactly what the law is and what the responsibility of the Dominion government would be in this matter, but I know that the Department of the Interior have had officers out there taking levels and looking into the matter, and I think something ought to be done. I have no doubt that this year the damages that have occurred to the farmers amount to something over half a million dollars. It is a serious thing. The loss is not so very serious to the province as a whole, but it is very serious to the people who live in that fertile valley. I do hope the minister will look into the matter and that something will be done.
I have much pleasure in endorsing the remarks of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.

I would like to ask
the minister about certain necessary work required in the region of Icelandic river. Has the minister decided to do any thing about that?

I have not that

Now I come to the point. The contract for the dry dock that we have asked for in Vancouver was entered into by the then Minister of Public Works, on behalf of the government of Canada, under the Dry-docks Subsidies Act, which was passed in 1910. One of the features of the election campaign was the unanimity of both parties on the point that above all things the dry dock in Vancouver would be proceeded with, no matter what party was returned to power. thing might happen in the event of the present Government being returned to office. Now, a dry dock is a business necessity. The member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) went into the details of this particular matter. I shall not do so, but im a word, I would urge upon the minister the importance of proceeding with this work. Ships leave this port for China, Japan, New Zealand, Australia, California, Mexico, South America and various places on the Pacific, and yet it is the only port of any considerable size in Canada without dry dock facilities. It is contended that sooner or later Victoria will have a dry dock that will provide for all our needs; but if I understand the situation rightly it will be four or five years before that dock is completed. The dock which it was contemplated to build at Vancouver would be completed, we understood, within a comparatively short time. I hope the Government will realize what it means to the people of Vancouver to have this dock built. We have guarding that great port, on the top of Crown mountain, two peaks having the appearance of crouching lions. They watch over the harbour, and I want to warn my hon. friends in the Government that these silent figures may make themselves heard before long. My hon. friends may hear their roar in a short while when the provincial elections come on. However, that is another side of the question; I am simply emphasizing the importance, from a purely business point of view, of proceeding with the construction of this dry dock. All the important organizations and public bodies throughout the lower mainland are at a loss to understand why the government of a great country like this can cancel a contract for such an undertaking in a city like Vancouver, the possible maximum liability being only about $112,000 a year. I have not the Ontario mileage. It is comparatively small.

Item agreed to.
St. John harbour-improvements, $850,000.

I would like to ask
whether the vote for St. John harbour is to be devoted entirely to the construction of Courtenay bay or whether the minister can hold out any hope that the very much needed work of extending the Negro Point breakwater to Partridge Island will be carried on this year.
I do not wish to take up much time, because I think the minister has some knowledge at all events of the gravity of that situation, and I am sure the officers of his department understand it thoroughly. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) was recently in St. John, and I am sure that from a personal inspection he too, has been impressed with the necessity of this work. The work of course, is necessarily a local one, because you cannot build a breakwater without a locality, but it is a most important work, not alone from the standpoint of the city which is in its vicinity, but from the viewpoint that the federal government has expended millions of dollars in digging out to a depth sufficient to float very large ocean steamships, a large space of territory between the breakwater and the present wharves. The government has also spent a large amount of money in providing very modern and first-class piers, but the outer berth at these piers is utterly impossible of utilization and the other two berths that lie between the piers can only be used under advantageous weather conditions. It means, that in the port of St. John, while we have very excellent though limited accommodation, we cannot count on being able to take advantage of that accommodation at all times during the winter. If there is a storm from the south of even moderate severity, it renders these berths simply impracticable for shipping and since the large dredging operations in Courtenay bay, I think the undertow on the west side has been increased. I am not asking to stop
any work in St. John harbour, but I would like very much to have the minister show an ability to hold out some hope that this very pressing necessity might be grappled with before next fall.
I believe the department once had under consideration, not an expensive means of doing the work, but a comparatively inexpensive means. At first the engineers insisted on having large granite blocks which would have to be quarried at some distance and brought, at a great cost to the site, but I know that more recently representations have been made that the stone of which Partridge island is composed would be perfectly good, if taken off in sufficiently large quantities, and by a very simple device it would be possible to transport that stone by means of an overhead cable and drop it into this gap, reducing the cost of construction to a minimum. I do not want to elaborate on how this thing can be done but I would like to know that the necessity of doing the work in what I might call the immediate future is engaging the attention of the Government, and I would also like to know whether the Government thinks it can see its way clear to carry on this work.

Might I add a word on the same subject? I would not urge the minister to undertake at the present time a work that is not imperative, but when a work is in my view absolutely imperative I would take the opportunity, as I do now, of impressing upon him the importance, not exactly of undertaking a new work, but the completion of an old work, and that is the extension of the Negro Point breakwater to which my colleague has just referred, to the adjacent island known as Partridge island. I am quite aware that the minister is familiar with the geography of the area I have mentioned, and it is at the request of the Board of Trade of St. John that I am bringing this matter for ward. I understand that the Board of Trade have also communicated with the minister direct in regard to this matter? Why do I urge this? I urge it for the protection of the wharves, of the shipping, and of the work in Courtenay bay-for the protection of all three. During stormy weather, as happened on more than one occasion last winter, the wharves on both sides of the harbour suffered considerable damage. Not only that, but several steamers suffered damage from being pounded against these wharves during the gale. Furthermore, gales have the result
Supply-Public Works

of washing sand into the area of Courtenay bay which is now being dredged for the provision of extensions for the Atlantic service, the sand coming in as the dredging is being done. I would therefore urge the minister to undertake this work as it is imperative to save property, as well as loss in connection with the work that is actually going on. The object, I think, will be clear to the House. The extension of the breakwater will prevent the seas washing into the harbour under the influence of winds coming from certain directions. I also should be pleased if the minister could give us some encouraging statement regarding this matter.

This amount of $850,000 is for the continuation of the work in Courtenay bay, and an amount of $65,000 will be required for maintenance and general repairs within the harbour. No provision has been made by the Government for the extension of the breakwater to which my hon. friends from St. John have been referring. Undoubtedly that is a work of great importance to the harbour and it will also involve a very considerable expenditure, but it is not the purpose of the Government to proceed with it this year.

If Mr. Pearson undertakes new work, such as the completion of the tower, that would have to be provided for. Probably my hon. friend is referring to some accounts now outstanding with Mr. Pearson. Will my hon. friend tell me who is responsible for the condition which obtains?

I will answer my hon. friend by saying this: If I had undertaken to do this work, and if the appropriation, under the contract as at first contemplated, was exhausted, and my employer told me to proceed and spend twice as much I would ask him for the payment of something on account. I would remind that employer of the provisions of the arrangement under which I was first employed and to which he was quite willing to agree when the contract was first undertaken. I have found Mr. Pearson to be a reasonable man. Furthermore, I am sure he does not have the least idea that I am saying one word on his behalf to-night; but I must say to the minister that I have heard this matter greatly talked about.
May I ask my hon. friend another question?

My hon. friend may ask any question he likes and I will answer it to the best of my ability, but I would like now to conclude what I have to say.
I have heard of it since I came to Ottawa, and I heard of it in the East and in the West. Surely, if this is a business government, they should get to work and reach some modus vivendi with the architect, and carry on until the building is completed. If an arrangement cannot be made with the architect, discharge him, get some other architect and go ahead. The statement that the late government was to blame is no answer. I am not trying to excuse them for any blame that may rest upon them in connection with this matter. I believe if this thing goes on, it will result in a scandal if this magnificent building which we admire so much, in which there is a spirit which cannot be found elsewhere, be left in an uncompleted condition.
Oh, oh.

My hon friends have taken a meaning out of my remarks which pleases them more than it occupies my mind. I was thinking of the nobility of this building and how it must impress every one who comes within its precincts. I say that it is a pity to have it go abroad that, by reason of this letter, which in law I submit is no defence, they are going to have a wrangle with the architect, that the building is not going to be completed, things are to remain at a standstill and the country is to suffer.

Was there not a contract let by the late government? If so, why was it that a dispute occurred between them and the architect? Why is my hon. friend so impatient and in such a hurry for the present administration, before they have had an opportunity to fully consider the case, to rectify a mistake made by the late government? The nobility of the building is not sufficient justification for the payment of enormous fees.

I think it would be well if the hon. member directed this question to the Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend is giving the matter a twist as I said nothing to warrant his remark. I have not suggested that one cent more than a fair and just remuneration should be paid. My point is that there is money owing, and if there is money owing, it should be paid.

I presume my hon.
friend is a lawyer, and if so, he must know that a person is bound by a written contract. If the architect guaranteed with the government of Canada to erect this building at a certain maximum cost, then why should he be paid for more than that cost?
I have seen the letter and the letter shows that my hon. friend's premises are incorrect.

I would ask the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) if he thinks there is a written contract which would justify the previous government in refusing to make a payment to the government architect, why he prefaces his remarks by an attempt to make it appear before the country that the late government did something wrong? Is it so absolutely necessary to sneer at the late government and belabour it on every occasion?

I think the committee should understand the position which exists today in regard to the Parliament Buildings, and the payment of the amount claimed by Mr. Pearson. When the buildings were first started an arrangement was made whereby a committee of this House, appointed by the leaders of the two parties, undertook to carry on the construction of this building. Up to date that work has been performed by this committee. Arrangements with the architect Were made with the knowledge of the committee, and when the cost began to exceed $5,000,000, a claim was made by Mr. Pearson for further commission. An investigation was made by that committee and they recommended that he should be paid a commission on some $2,000,000, in addition to the five million that had been expended. That is the recommendation that is before the Public Works Department to-day. As hon. member's may understand, many members of the committee that acted up to December of last year are not now in Parliament, and there is to-day no committee. As far as the Public Works Department is concerned, we have certain recommendations and minutes coming from this committee which suggests a fair settlement with Mr. Pearson. Mr. Pearson has not seen fit to accept the suggestion of that committee. He is contending for a larger commission, rightly or wrongly. Up to date commissions have been paid, to Mr. Pearson, to the amount of some $289,000
fMr. Ryckman.]
and to Mr. Marchand some $52,000, making a total of $342,000 paid in architects' commissions. The hon. member from East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) suggested that the Government should issue a fiat. As far as we are concerned we have no great objection, if that is the wish, to issue a fiat, and let Mr. Pearson go to court. It is true suggestions have been made that we should get together and arrive at something that would be equitable and fair. Personally, I take the position, as far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, that in taking over this work that was formerly under the control of a committee of Parliament, we must, at least, accept their suggestion in matters with which they had been dealing up to the time the committee ceased to exist. That is the position of the claim to-day. It is receiving further consideration. I may, in the course of a few days, make some recommendation to the Government in regard to it.

What is the intention of the Department of Public Works regarding the tower? An item appeared in the press stating that it was the intention riot to proceed any further with the building of the tower. Is the minister ready to make a statement with regard to that?
It is- not proposed to continue the construction of the tower this year. We may ask to have plans prepared with a view to going on next session.

I was not in any sense levelling an attack at the present minister who has been in his office such a short time.
I was hoping that I would have from the minister an assurance-which I think the minister has given me, and which I hope I can take as an assurance-that this matter will be taken up and remedied at as early a date as possible.
Can the minister give us any information as to why the building has cost so much more than was intended . in the first place?

The building is more elaborate and much larger than intended in the first place, and we are all familiar with the increase in cost of material and supplies generally. I think that would account for the great increase in cost.

That is to he
done.

There is a contract with the firm of Peter Lyall and Sons on a percentage, or force account basis.
