speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of the Department of Health) :
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health

I should like to ask the minister a rather pertinent question; in fact, perhaps, somebody might call it impertinent. The statement is often made, in the press of a certain type at least, that the drug habit in this country is increasing -and I think I am right in stating that it is increasing, according to the number of prosecutions which the minister has men-
Supply-Public Health

tioned-by virtue of the fact that temperance or prohibition measures have been taken in different provinces of this Dominion. I presume that such men as Doctor Amyot, the ^deputy minister, and other able officers in this department, have opinions on the matter which they have expressed to the minister. I am sure that the committee will be pleased to have a statement from the minister on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is imposing a considerable task upon me. I am indeed not in a position to furnish any information in this regard. Whether the use of alcohol would tend to abate to any extent the illicit desire for drugs, it is not for me to say. My impression, however, is that it makes no difference.

The minister could
ascertain from the provincial returns whether there was a smaller percentage of prosecutions for the illicit use of drugs in British Columbia and in Montreal or Quebec than elsewhere. These two provinces are what are known commonly as " wet " territories, and if the prosecutions there were markedly less than elsewhere the suggestion would have some foundation, that the use of alcohol has a restrictive effect on the use of drugs.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am afraid that if that were true, British Columbia would be amply justified in having indulged in the liquor trade, because the number of convictions in the matter of drugs is a good deal larger there than elsewhere. But I do not believe that the liquor habit and the drug habit have very much relation to each other. It is true that in British Columbia the liquor traffic is permitted under certain legislative regulations, and it is equally true that it is in that province that the largest number of convictions for the illicit use of drugs have taken place. But the large number of convictions against illicit traders in narcotics in British Columbia would, I should think, naturally result from the geographic situation of that province. I presume that there is a larger number of Chinamen in Vancouver and Victoria than in any other city in the Dominion, and the proximity of these places to the Orient would perhaps account for the greater extent of the trade.

I do not wish to be understood as making the statement that the increase in the use of drugs is due to any corresponding decrease in the use of

alcohol. I simply state that a portion of the press frequently makes that statement, and I thought in all seriousness that perhaps some of the officials of the department might have given a positive opinion on the matter. The minister, I think, did state that there was an increasing use of these drugs, which I take it include not only opium but morphine, cocaine and the various other habit-forming drugs, and possibly the number of prosecutions may be due to a stricter enforcement of the law. I may have misunderstood the minister, but I thought he said that it was the opinion of the department that the use of these drugs is on the increase. If that is the case-and the minister nods his head-would he be willing to give the opinion of some of his officers as to the cause of the increase? Or has any such opinion been expressed to him by the officers of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am unable to give any reasons for the apparent increase. As my hon. friend, who is conversant with medical matters, knows, it is very difficult to say whether the use of narcotics has really increased. Apparently it has, and this may foe due to the fact that the department has been very closely prosecuting the illicit traders. But we have no report in the department that assigns any reasons for the increase. Possibly, as in some other lines, the traders have found it very profitable to deal in these drugs, and the habit has spread among some of our compatriots, and is practised by more foreigners than in previous years. I can only say that it is most regrettable that the trade should have reached such proportions, and that is one reason why we shall require a little more money to bring to the enforcement of this act as much activity as possible.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which I think is very important. The committee will have noted that in the number of prosecutions a very large percentage were aliens. I believe that a very considerable proportion of them were orientals. In British Columbia, where we realize, more than any other part of the country does, the connection between Canada and the Orient in the supplying of these drugs, and where we have been right up against the problem, so to speak, we have been asking that those found guilty and convicted in our courts shall wherever possible be de

Supply-Public Health
ported. Nothing is so feared by a criminal practising in Canada as deportation back to the land whence he came. That is true generally speaking. There is nothing that the Chinaman in particular dreads so much as deportation. If the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) were in his place I would address a few remarks to him, but I trust that my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) will renew his conferences with him on this point. One of the heaviest blows that could be struck at the traffic would be a vigorous campaign of deportation. As the law now stands it requires that those prosecuting shall notify the municipal clerk who in turn notifies the immigration authorities. I am not criticising the law, but it does strike me that the Department of Health could, as it were, short circuit this red tape by having the representations made direct to the Immigration Department, who could actively take the matter up. As matters stand now, the Immigration Department does not act until the charge is laid by the municipal authority, whereas, if the Health Department, cooperating with the Immigration Department, were to notify immediately a prosecution was made, then the immigration authorities could follow the matter up. And if the Government would instruct the immigration authorities to take vigorous action it would go a long way towards remedying the evil.
Another matter I wish to refer to is the spread of the drug habit. From our experiences and careful investigations made, I think that the chief cause lies in the profit which is made by unscrupulous- I was going to say fiendish-traffickers. They are the root of this business, and it is encouraging to see the efforts made by the department of my hon. friend to prosecute these traffickers. But I think another step could be taken with pronounced effect. I have some papers on this point, but they are not under my hand at the moment. As, however, the minister will no doubt have full information in his department, what I say will be quite intelligible to him. Nearly all the civilized nations of the world, realizing that this traffic is getting a firmer grip upon their peoples, have entered into an international convention to restrict the traffic. As I understand it, the main source of supply for opium is the Orient, and for the derivatives of opium-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Cocaine and morphine.
Those come chiefly from Germany, although to a certain extent from France also.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is right.

Here we have the two major sources of supply. I think Canada might very well initiate steps to prevent the exports of drugs generally from those countries to Canada except under strict regulations. Germany has been a serious offender in this respect. I do not know that the government of Germany wilfully permits the export of these drugs, but at the same time she has been neglectful in the matter, and I think we might very properly make strong representations not only to Germany but to all the other countries which participated in this international convention, to control the export of these drugs as effectively as possible. As a matter of fact, I think the minister will agree with me when I say that if we could control the manufacture and export of these drugs we would go a long way towards solving the problem. India and China are undoubtedly sources of supply. In the old Chinese government at Pekin we had a very sympathetic ally in the control of opium exports, but I am afraid that what we might call the de facto government at Canton is not attempting to control these exports at all so far as we can learn. Very strong efforts ought to be made not only by Canada but by the other signatories to the convention to curtail, and, if possible, prevent the production and export of drugs.

Before the minister replies to the remarks of my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), may I add a word or two? Perhaps not having the papers under his hand my hon. friend has expressed his opinions a little differently from what he really wished to do, because after all, as the minister well knows, morphine particularly, as well as cocaine to a lesser extent, are very useful drugs if properly handled.
Yes.
Perhaps there is no drug more useful, generally speaking, than opium and its derivatives, and I presume that my hon. friend really suggests the prohibition of illegitimate exportation-
Undoubtedly.

-because the prohibition of legitimate exportation of drugs from those countries might interfere very ma-
Supply-Public Health

terially with the practice of medicine. As I understood him, the danger really comes from the smuggling of these drugs into Canada, and if some method were adopted which, instead of prohibiting, would secure strict registration of such exportations to our country, these records could be given to our customs officers, who could pass them on to the officers of my hon. friend's department, and the same result would be achieved. In regard to the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman as to the deportation of peddlers of these drugs, I think it is very good.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The committee will have an idea of how the legitimate trade in drugs has decreased in this country when I quote the figures for cocaine importations for 1919, 1920 and 1921. In 1919 we imported 12,000 ounces; in 1920, 6,900 ounces; in 1921, only 3,300 ounces. So in the last three years the legitimate importations have dropped from 12,000 ounces to 3,000 ounces. The same applies to morphine and to gum opium. One reason why these drugs are being absorbed in larger quantities is no doubt because through illicit trading they are sold a good deal cheaper. During the last three or four years the rigid enforcement of the law has prevented drug addicts from buying these narcotics so easily as they used to, and as illicit traders were in a position to offer the drugs at a cheaper price, the committee will readily understand that a much larger consumption has taken place.
I agree largely with what my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has said about deportation. It can be readily understood that if Chinamen who indulge in the illicit trade in narcotics, especially opium, were deported, others would be deterred from taking a similar risk, and the trading would be very much restricted. That is a matter for the special consideration of the Minister of the Interior and also of the Government generally.
The control of export from the country of origin is perhaps a more serious matter. It would be possible for the signatories to the convention entered into in 1912, and ratified by Canada in 1919, to enter into negotiations with the view of ascertaining the exact quantity of drugs exported from every country. That would be perhaps a very useful step to take.

I believe the convention contains a provision for exactly that course to be pursued, and what I am urging is
that the Government should take advantage of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Every country which is a party to that international convention undoubtedly would be ready to supply this Government with figures of the exact export trade in all these narcotics. But my hon. friend will realize also that there exists in those countries an export trade which is outside the law.

The minister gave the
total number of convictions as 835. Does that cover all convictions in Canada, not only those that have taken place through the efforts of the Department of Health, but through the ordinary channels of the enforcement of criminal law?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No. The total number of convictions is 1,765, which includes provincial and municipal prosecutions followed by conviction. The total number of convictions secured through federal prosecution is 835.

The total number of convictions, including those which have resulted through the ordinary channels of criminal prosecution, is 1,765. It is most significant that of the 835 convictions, no less than 634 are convictions of Chinese residing in Canada. So the total number of convictions of citizens of all other nationalities, Canadians and others, is only 201. This would lead one to conclude that this illicit traffic in drugs is, to the extent of at least sixty or sixty-six per cent, due to the presence in this country of a substantial Chinese population. I was inclined to think that during the past five years there had been a very large increase in the number of convictions that had taken place in Canada on account of the traffic in illicit drugs. When I was in the Department of Justice the matter was brought to my attention on more than one occasion, and though I cannot give the figures from memory now, I am inclined to think the increase in the number of convictions in the last five years has been very, very rapid. From an examination of the figures given us to-night, I think we may fairly assume that a very large part of that illicit traffic is conducted by people whose presence in this country is no great asset, in my humble opinion. I sincerely trust that the department will continue its good work. It is doing an excellent work in this respect, as are also the mounted police and the provincial police, but I am just a little bit afraid from what I read in the papers

Supply-Public Health
published in the United States, particularly in New York, that the traffic is on the increase and not on the decrease, both in Canada and the United States at the present time.

detained, was unable to reach home in time to get in a fair amount of crop, or at any rate such as he deemed necessary. It developed that he was not suffering from any contagious disease and I wondered what the attitude of the authorities was in a case of that nature?

the United States and Canada, I mean for those travellers or immigrants, who come from the former country and are recognized as American citizens; because we take it for granted that having been admitted by the United States inspectors after inspection, the conditions would be such as to entitle them to admission into Canada. realize that possibly I am not in order in bringing forward such a matter on this item, but the fact is that the Pension Committee, of which I am a member, sits afternoons and evenings when the House is in session, and I may not be here when the items referred to by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) are taken up. I would like to ask the minister if the Government has any intention of subsidizing a line of steamers between St. John, N.B., and Cuba, at any future time, and I want to state my reasons for asking the question. Last year I took up with the government the matter of seeing if some arrangement could not be made to facilitate the shipping of potatoes to Cuba, due to the fact that the United States tariff on potatoes, and other farm produce going to that country, is such that the market there is practically closed to us. The farmers of New Brunswick to-day are realizing only 40 cents a barrel for their potatoes, whereas the cost to them of raising those potatoes is $2 a barrel. On the average that is what it cost them to produce potatoes last year. Now, when the farmer is only getting 40 cents a barrel it means that he realizes but $120 for a car after the payment of freight, whereas the expense of landing these potatoes in Cuba is $550 a car, which is rather a hard situation for the farmers, as every hon. member must admit. These potatoes are shipped from St. John by boat, and I would like to know whether the Government would not consider the desirability of providing better facilities for handling them at the port of St. John, and of granting a subsidy to a line of steamers whereby we might get our potatoes to market at a reduced rate and in that way, so to speak, lessen the cost of production. I would like the Government to consider what might be done to meet the existing situation. It was proposed last year that the Government Merchant Marine should put on a line of steamers between St. John and Cuba, but it would be necessary that the vessels should be fitted up in such a way that potatoes could be carried without injury. The necessity of this arises from the fact that the holds of the ships are so arranged that when loaded with potatoes the sacks in the lower tier get crushed by the sacks in the tier above. The facilities between decks should be such that no injury would result from this cause. I got the Dominion Merchant Marine to handle shipments on their boats in 1920, but when landed in Cuba some were in very 
bad condition due to the fact that the potatoes in the top tiers had crushed those in the lower tiers so badly that they were not marketable. I took the matter up last year with the Department of Marine and they told me the reason they would not be able to meet our wishes was because there were not enough potatoes offering at the port of St. John to enable such cargoes to be carried at a profit. Well, the reason for that is that our potatoes were going via Boston where there are better facilities for handling them than at the port of St. John. The Minister of Public Works agreed this session, as the result of a resolution I introduced into the House to endeavour to provide export facilities at the port of St. John. When that has been attended to we shall need some adequate means of transporting our potatoes to Cuba so that they may be landed there at a reduced rate of freight and without injury, thus enabling our farmers to realize a larger amount than they at present receive.
If my hon. friend will give me a memorandum on the subject I shall be pleased to take the matter up with the department.

Quebec, Natashquan and Harrington, and Bras d'Or and other ports on the north shore of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, steam service between, $85,000.
We would like some information on this?
Thi6 is a considerable increase. The service will extend 300 miles further east, giving a service to Canadian ports, and bringing back to Canadian ports business that now goes to Newfoundland.
Are any of the Canadian Merchant Marine vessels employed on this service?
No.
What service are we going to get? What ships are employed? This is an enormous increase, from $50,000 to $85,000.
We are putting on new ships and a new service, giving an increased service over that of last year, between Harrington and the other points.
Will the hon. minister allow it to stand?

Yes.
Item stands.
St. Catherine's Bay and Tadoussac, winter steam service between, $2,000.
What about the winter service at that point?
This is a new service. These people are completely isolated during the winter, so that they have no way of getting the mail sent in.
How are they going to do it?
The mails are carried by dog trains down to a certain point, and there will be a ferry service across from St. Catherine to Tadoussac.

What is the meaning of "winter steam service"?

It means that the service
will apply only in the winter time, when the mails cannot get in otherwise. In the season of navigation, there is another service.

Item agreed to.
St. John and St. Andrews, N.B., calling at intermediate points, steam service between, $4,000.

This is a service that
cannot be justified on the ground that it carries mail. The boat is a local freight boat owned by a firm at Black harbour, and travelling between St. John and St. Andrews. I do not want to be taken as opposing this appropriation; but I should like to know the justification for the subsidy, because this boat does not carry a single mail bag.

If my hon. friend desires
that the item stand, we shall allow it to stand for further information.
Let us have the information later on. I would not ask that the item stand.

Item agreed to.
St. John and Digby, steam service between, $15,000.

This is a Canadian
Pacific service, which is very well patronized. The boat is a good one, which carries a large tourist traffic in the summer. What is the justification for the apparently large increase? I do not see any necessity for an increase on this service which has been established for many years. This boat carries also a considerable quantity of freight.

I will allow this item to
stand if my hon. friend so desires. My recollection is that this is an increased service.
There is a daily service now. Is the company putting on two trips a day?

Perhaps the item had
better stand until I have the information.
Item stands.
St. Stephen, Deer Island, and Campobello, steam service between, $2,000.

This is a very inadequate service; in fact, it is not a steam service at all. The boat is a gasoline one. Possibly there have been applications for an improved service. In the winter time the boat is not fit for passenger service.

There may have been applications for an increased service. Many applications have been made for increased services and increased subsidies. We propose to make a thorough review during the coming season and perhaps, we shall correct the services, increasing some and reducing others.
This service could be very well increased.

Item agreed to.
Sydney and Whycocomagh, steam service between, $7,000.
This appropriation is nearly doubled. We ought to have some explanation.

My recollection is that this boat showed very bad earnings during the last two years, and that the company were about to discontinue the service altogether, a service which was necessary for the people of this district. Otherwise, they would have no way of getting their produce to market.
Will the minister let this stand?
I will.

The minister tells
us that they threathened to discontinue the service. Is this let by contract? Has the minister any guarantee of continuity of service where a subsidy is granted?

These services are voted each year, and sometimes we give these companies contracts covering a term of years. But when they come forward with a statement showing that they are making great losses, it is often cheaper to cancel a contract than to attempt to make them carry out a contract when they are unable to do it.

I am finding no fault with the increase of the subsidy, if that is found necessary on account of their producing a statement of their earnings. Has the department any guarantee of continuity of service for a definite time? When liberal subsidies are granted, there should be more than a yearly contract.
There are in many cases. There are but few defaults.

I should like this to stand for further information.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am able to give the committee any quantity of information about this service, which must be about a hundred years old. The boat is a good many years old; but the company are getting a new steel boat this year, and that is the cause of the increase. The new boat is costing them something like $40,000, whereas the old boat was not so expensive. The old boat was getting a subsidy of only $4,000. The distance between Whycoco-magh and Sydney is eighty miles. The boat is on the road all the time, going one day and coming back the next, going back and forth continuously, making calls all the way along the Bras d'Or lake. There is no railroad on that side of the island, and this boat answers the purpose. There are many wharves on the lake, and the boat carries freight and passengers back and forth. We could not get along without the service.

The minister stated
that he had statements from the company showing that they were losing money. I think the committee ought to have those statements in order to see how the matter stands. The minister might let this item stand over until he can furnish the committee with the statements.

I do not see why this item should stand any more than any other item. If the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) thinks that, because this service is in my constituency, he is doing a great thing by holding over this estimate, we might stay here for a while and get the information. This item has been passed yearly for the last twenty years since I came to this House, and I never before heard a request that it should stand over. There should be no trouble in getting these statements showing that they were losing money, because I was present in the office when the captain of the boat and the president of the company made them to the minister. If the hon. gentleman thinks he is doing a great service to his country by stopping this item simply because the service is in my riding, I suppose he can do that; but it is a long lane that has no turning.

My hon. friend is assuming a great deal. He says that we are stopping an item 'because it refers to a service in his riding. I do not think that anyone knew, when the request was made, that the matter referred to my hon. friend's riding. Certainly I did not know. But
here is an increase from $4,000 to $7,000. The minister says he has explanations which he will bring forward. We simply ask that the item stand, entirely apart from the fact that it refers to the riding of the Solicitor General. The hon. gentleman need not get angry.
I am not angry; there is no reason why I should be. Only protests or arguments from a gentleman would make me angry.
The committee is entitled to the information; I think the item should stand.
We have been doing very nicely and we have asked that just four items out of some forty be allowed to stand. I do not think the request is unreasonable.
The temper of the committee is getting bad.

We have not made the request for the purpose of humiliating my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), who is beyond that, anyway.
Item stands.
Sydney and Bras d'Or Lake ports and ports on the east and west coasts of Cape Breton, steam service between, $14,000.
How many services are there in connection with this item?
There are quite a number of them; different services around points where there is no railway communication.

Item agreed to.
To provide for a Canadian Exhibition in France, $50,000.
What are the particulars?

Last year Senator Beaubien arranged with France that in consideration of Canada giving free transportation to their products over our railways France would give in return free transportation and certain other concessions to an exhibit of Canadian products throughout that country. To take advantage of that arrangement it is well that we should take steps now, while the same government are in office in France, and 'before they forget the matter. We propose to send an exhibit of Canadian agricultural and industrial products to France.

Personally, I have no
desire to delay the vote at all. In fact I am wholly in favour of it, and I state
2032	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
frankly that I think it will be of great benefit to those Canadians who are interested in the French market. I think that an exhibition of a Canadian train in France would be of great advantage to us. We should do all we can to promote trade between the two countries, and I heartily endorse the vote. I know a good deal about it and I am entirely in favour of the scheme.

How is the $50,000
arrived at?

It is purely an estimate.
The negotiations with France were carried out by Senator Beaubien. It may require more than $50,000 but we are putting in this item in the hope that we shall receive some assistance from the Canadian Manufacturers Association.
I understand that France imports very little farm produce from any country. What are her agricultural imports from Canada?

We can obtain that information, but my hon. friend is wrong. France has bought considerable amounts of Canadian products, and we hope to be able to increase the sales. If France were buying all the products we have to sell, it would be unnecessary, of course, to send an exhibit there and advertise our products. It is because we wish to increase Canadian business in that market, particularly our agricultural products, that we are taking this matter up.
Agricultural products, or implements?
Both; I hope my hon. friend does not object to our selling agricultural implements in France.

It is because I doubt the
existence of that market that I ask the question.

There are other business
men in Canada who hold a different opinion from my hon. friend.
Will the Government get some assistance from the Canadian Manufacturers Association?

We hope they will contribute in part to the expenses. We will arrange for the train and for a suitable building in which to display our products. We may possibly also arrange for a permanent exhibition there, and those who are interested may contribute by supplying products.

It seems rather strange
that we should put a tariff on French goods and France impose one against us in order to keep out trade, and then we should turn round and spend $50,000 in order to get trade in.

It is not the policy of this
Government to keep trade out or to discourage it.
Is the minister considering a mutual arrangement with France for a reduction in the tariff? The money would be better spent in that way than, perhaps, under this item.

If my hon. friend will
have patience possibly some day we will give the information he desires.

I understood that
France imported very few agricultural products; in fact, my information was that the French law prohibited their importation. At the present time I am informed that France produces all the agricultural commodities she requires. I understood, though, that there is a chance of doing business there in manufactured goods. It is probably more particularly for that purpose that this exhibition is to be held. I am not opposing the grant, but I was curious to know how this $50,000 was made up-whether the exhibitors were charged a certain amount and the Government was contributing the balance; and also whether agricultural products are to be put on exhibition as well as manufactured goods.

The item was arrived at, as already explained, purely by estimate. We propose to have an exhibition of agricultural products, minerals, manufactured goods-in fact, everything Canada produces that we think can be sold in France. My hon. friends must keep in mind that France is one of the great tourist countries of the world, and therefore the exhibits Canada shows will be seen by the people of other nations.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING moved the adjournment of the House.

May I inquire whether my hon. friend has considered the question of sitting on Saturdays? A number of

Business of the House
members on both sides of the House have been discussing it during the last day or two, and I 'think myself that the time has come when we should deal with it. I should also like to know the business for Monday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I assume from my hon. friend's remarks that he hopes the Government will do everything in its power to expedite the work, so as to bring the session to a close as soon as possible. Certainly the Government has under consideration what may be possible towards that end. The coming week the House does not sit on Wednesday and Thursday. Some suggestion was made by an hon. member two or three days ago that we might sit on Saturdays, but there seemed to be considerable difference of opinion at the time, and for the Saturday of next week the suggestion did not seem to meet with general approval. The Government would be only too glad to sit on Saturdays if that course were generally approved by the House.
The House will sit on Friday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes; and if between now and Tuesday it should appear that there is a general sentiment in favour of sitting on Saturday I am sure the Government will be glad to meet the wishes of hon. members in that regard. After the following Wednesday we will resume sittings in the evening. If there is any sentiment in favour of sitting on Saturdays we shall be glad to consider the advisability of doing so.
I hope the Government will not sit next Saturday. After that date I should have no objection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We will be all ready to sit next Saturday if there is any agreement to do so.
May we take it that the custom established by the Government at the commencement of the session of rising at eleven o'clock is not to be abandoned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no, I do not think it will be abandoned. If there is a disposition on the part of members to get through the balance of the work of the session by not speaking at too great length, I do not see why we should not adjourn at eleven o'clock as usual; but if for any reason there is a tendency to delay matters unduly, the Government will probably feel justified in continuing the sittings a little later than eleven o'clock to get through a good day's work. When we can get through reasonably by eleven o'clock, we shall be glad to do so. [DOT]

I am asking the question because several members leave towards eleven o'clock under the impression that the House will rise at that hour, but lately we have been sitting until twelve o'clock or later.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As to the business for Monday, we will take what remains of naval and militia estimates, mounted police, soldiers' land settlement, adjustment of war claims, fisheries, and any other estimates on the list.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.55 p.m.
